level2: The Saab JAS 39 Gripen is a multirole fighter manufactured by Swedish aerospace company Saab AB.
The Swedish designation JAS stands for Jakt, Attack, and Spaning, signifying its versatile mission profile.
In contrast to previous Cold War interceptors, the Gripen performs fighter, strike, and reconnaissance roles on a single mission.
The aircraft features an inherently unstable aerodynamic configuration with delta wings and controllable canard foreplanes.
Digital fly-by-wire flight control computers continuously adjust control surfaces to maintain stability and agility.
Pilots wear pressurized anti-g suits to prevent gravity-induced loss of consciousness during high-speed turns.
The Gripen was engineered to operate from standard eight hundred meter road strips under the Swedish Bas 90 doctrine.
An on-board auxiliary power unit allows the jet to start its engine independently without external ground support carts.
Mobile conscript maintenance teams can turn around and rearm an incoming fighter in just ten minutes on a highway.
Infrared search and track sensors allow pilots to passively locate targets without broadcasting radar emissions.
The cockpit features three full-color multi-function displays presenting tactical radar and navigation maps.
Precision guided munitions allow high-altitude strikes against tactical positions while minimizing collateral damage.

level3: During the Cold War, the Swedish Air Force was ranked among the largest and most technologically capable air fleets in the world, maintaining strict armed neutrality.
The Saab 35 Draken introduced the revolutionary double-delta wing planform, allowing supersonic dash capability while retaining docile handling during low-speed landings.
The Saab 37 Viggen pioneered canard aerodynamics and reverse-thrust landing mechanisms, allowing heavy attack aircraft to land on narrow Swedish highway runways in winter conditions.
The Bas 90 wartime dispersal strategy divided air bases into main runways and secondary kortbanor, scattering flight divisions across hundreds of forest road strips to survive preemptive strikes.
Data links form the tactical backbone of Swedish air defense, allowing Gripens to share radar tracks, target coordinates, and weapon assignments silently between aircraft without vocal radio calls.
The Flygvapnet participates routinely in multinational Arctic Challenge exercises, demonstrating rapid deployment, aerial refueling, and coalition interoperability alongside NATO partners.
Airborne early warning and control aircraft, such as the Saab GlobalEye, provide long-range maritime and airspace radar surveillance across the Baltic Sea region.
Supersonic aerodynamics require careful management of shockwaves and wave drag, utilizing area rule fuselage design to smooth high-speed airflow past the wings and canards.
level4: The Gripen C is powered by a Volvo Aero RM12 turbofan, a license-built derivative of the General Electric F404, delivering 54 kN of dry thrust and 80.5 kN with afterburner engaged.
The Ericsson PS-05/A multi-mode pulse-Doppler radar operates in the X-band between 8 and 10 GHz, featuring look-down/shoot-down tracking and synthetic aperture ground mapping capabilities.
With a maximum takeoff weight of 14,000 kg and an empty weight of 6,800 kg, the Gripen achieves a thrust-to-weight ratio exceeding 1.0, enabling a top speed of Mach 2.0 at 12,000 meters altitude.
The modernized Gripen E incorporates a General Electric F414G powerplant generating 98 kN of wet thrust, allowing supercruise at Mach 1.25 without consuming fuel in fuel-hungry afterburner stage.
The Leonardo Raven ES-05 active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar utilizes an innovative 'swashplate' mechanical repositioner, granting an unprecedented +/- 100 degree field of regard.
The internal Mauser BK-27 mm revolver cannon fires up to 1,700 rounds per minute, supplemented by eight external hardpoints capable of carrying up to 5,300 kg of precision ordnance.
level5: Armed with MBDA's ramjet-powered Meteor BVRAAM (Beyond-Visual-Range Air-to-Air Missile), the Gripen boasts a 'No Escape Zone' exceeding 60+ km - three times greater than conventional solid-fuel AIM-120 AMRAAMs.

The Gripen's close-coupled canard configuration induces strong aerodynamic vortices across the delta wing's upper surface, delaying boundary-layer stall at extreme angles of attack (AoA > 35°) and generating instantaneous pitch rates in excess of 30°/s.

During Red Flag 2006 at Nellis AFB, Nevada, Swedish Gripens from F 17 Kallinge utilized the TIDLS (Tactical Information Data Link System) to coordinate silent pincer ambushes against 4th-Gen aggressor F-16Cs, achieving multiple simulated 'Fox-3' kills with zero radar emission alerts.

The upgraded E-series cockpit features a Panoramic Wide Area Display (WAD) measuring 19 x 8 inches (48 x 20 cm) with 3840 x 1280 resolution, driven by multi-core AdaCore DO-178C avionics running real-time partition-separated mission computers.

Tactical electronic warfare suite EWS-39 incorporates Gallium Nitride (GaN) digital radio frequency memory (DRFM) jammers and missile approach warning sensors (MAWS), countering modern VHF and phased-array SAMs such as S-400 'Triumf' (NATO: SA-21 'Growler').
